basis: The older John Glasgow who held the Saltmarket Rankin–Young tenement in 1527 is assessed as the probable father of William Glasgow-1098. William occupies the matching parcel by 20 February 1528/29; the later St Andrew prebend rental retains its four-shilling burden, west-side street position and Rankin boundary. The 1534 family settlement and 1564 service as heir then directly identify the younger John Glasgow-1093 as William’s son. Read together, these describe a sustained family title rather than merely two men sharing a surname. Lineal succession from the earlier John to William is the preferred reconstruction, while the last William-to-John step is independently documented. The grade is now probable, below documented or strongly supported. This brings the formal local father assessment into line with the stronger property argument already developed in the research.

A brother, collateral heir or purchase from a namesake remains possible. Indeed, the neighbouring Henryson parcel in the 1528/29 instrument passes between brothers; title succession alone cannot specify kinship. The combined parcel descriptions are correlated, and the later rental is not an independent record of the original transfer. Glasgow-1095 remains a provisional representation of the Saltmarket owner: its identification with the Stirling witness or the 1506 alias-Smith purchaser is not proved. The probable grade applies to the property-defined Saltmarket father hypothesis, not to every imported biographical claim. No mother is inferred: Eufame Craig may have been the earlier John’s widow, but this does not establish her as William’s mother. No Stirling parent, birth estimate, death location or identity merge is upgraded. The live WikiTree father flag remains uncertain; probable is a local research grade.

claim: Andrew Glasgow of Calder is the selected uncertain working father of James Glasgow.
basis: Andrew’s documented rural Calder household is the preferred working anchor for James’s nearby Mid Calder family. He was alive across the estimated1575–1586 birth interval of all three Lothian fathers; Hermand John’s1577 death would require an earlier birth estimate for David. That favours this coherent provisional family without excluding the other father. Andrew was alive until1598 and the uncertain generations allow James to be an older son. This uses the actual Calder setting and compatible family sequence, not the withdrawn assertion that the testament named James. James’s Inveresk/Fisherrow identity remains a separate uncertainty.
limitations: John of Hermand-3181 is another plausible older local father. The George named at Mureistoun1586 and the George witness1605 are a competing father/relative lead; identifying that George with merchant1099 would require additional identity assumptions and young fatherhood. None is excluded. Andrew’s omission of James weakens this model; it does not disprove an older son. Confidence review, 16 October 2026: the Mureistoun George of 1586 is now probably the 1605 adult witness, through the same-holding household association and compatible interval. That strengthens the local George comparison; his exact relationship to James remains unknown. It does not identify the witness with merchant Glasgow-1099 or document Andrew as father.

Glasgow-991.reason: Earlier Andrew placement retained as alternative. The 1605 witness’s residence and age are unstated, and Muirestoun remains a probable reading/location. Shared holding names do not prove a legal title transfer. Father, uncle, older brother, cousin and neighbour remain genuine alternatives. The 1586 obligation does not establish muster attendance, and neither record states that George was James’s father. The George name and witness role are supporting context, not direct kinship. Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains an unselected uncertain father alternative; his 1597/8 testament names Robert, Marion, Jonet and Isobel, not James. The George comparison supplies a closer holding-and-witness association than the broader Andrew/Calder model, without proving that Andrew could not be James’s father.

claim: The earlier Corsankell John is selected as the Saltcoats sailor’s uncertain father.
basis: Select John Glasgow-3193, the recorded son at Corsankell in 1571 and probable Kilwinning tenant of 1559–60, as the Saltcoats sailor John Glasgow-4152’s uncertain working father. Saltcoats in Ardrossan adjoins the Stevenston–Kilwinning coastal parish cluster where this earlier Glasgow family is documented. A later-sixteenth-century son of the earlier adult could have been a working sailor and father of two daughters by 1636. The choice gives the Saltcoats household a provisional place in an existing local John line, using geography and a feasible generation. It is a low-confidence selection, not a named parent clause or an identification of the two Johns.
limitations: No source names the sailor’s parents or age. His former c.1600 birth was an unsupported creation estimate; it is not replaced by an invented older birth to fit this hypothesis. If a birth near 1600 is eventually established, the earlier John would have been an older father, and a grandson or more distant collateral placement could be more natural. Same given name is weak support and does not distinguish this candidate securely from Glasgow-3921 (James younger), another member of the local family, or an unrecorded father. The sailor could belong elsewhere in that family or to another branch. The 1559–60 Kilwinning attribution to the Corsankell John is itself probable, although the 1571 Corsankell family is directly recorded. The same-person alternative is less economical: an adult in 1559 would have been about 95 or older at the sailor’s death in 1636, assuming adulthood at eighteen. That is an illustrative age comparison, not a proved exclusion. The father-versus-grandfather degree remains open. No mother is assigned to the sailor or to his daughters; Agnes Wilson’s joint tenancy does not make her his mother, and Isobell Gray’s widowhood does not prove her maternity. claim: Selected uncertain father for James Glasgow, Quothquan weaver
basis: Select Stephen Glasgow-1029 as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-3910. James’s weaver occupation and Quothquan locality favour using the 1612 court defender and the 1624 testator as one working adult account. Stephen is documented as an adult in Glasgow in 1575 and with wife Margaret Grahame in 1582; his approximate 1550 birth is an estimate, not a birth record. The existing tree already places John Glasgow-3296, the 1650 Quothquan testator, under Stephen, uncertain. The preferred model treats the two early Quothquan men as paternal brothers rather than making the later John James’s father. A Stephen born around the mid-sixteenth century could have fathered James in the 1570s–1590s and John in a similar generation. This uses a named family already connected to Quothquan, at very low confidence, rather than inventing a missing parent. No record names Stephen as James’s father or James and John as brothers.
limitations: The route depends both on the proposed James–John brotherhood and on John’s already uncertain Stephen parentage. The Glasgow–Montfoid–Mid Calder–Quothquan identities are not proved migrations. John’s 1650 testament names his sister Bessie and no child or parent; omission of James, already dead by 1624, does not disprove brotherhood. John himself could instead be James’s father if older than his inherited estimate, or the men could be uncle/nephew, cousins or unrelated local namesakes. The older John and Thomas tenants in the 1520s–1530s remain possible ancestral relatives with unproved intervening generations; no direct father edge to them is selected. Margaret Grahame is Stephen’s documented spouse in 1582, not a documented mother of James, so no mother is attached. John’s existing mother field and all earlier parent and identity alternatives remain unchanged. Two selected uncertain local fathers; no new mother, original-source inspection, live WikiTree edit, identity merge or certainty upgrade. The family placements use existing record reviews, named local accounts and checked chronology; paternal/full sibling status remains conditional. Neither the record nor the profile supplies a real age, so this is not a recorded birthday or a hard biological exclusion. The 1607–1608 acts concern the earlier dispute, not a newly established birth or exact adult-age observation. The 26 July 1624 date is a testament confirmation, so death is shown as before that date and its place is left unresolved; Quothquan is the stated residence. Imported profile values remain in the comparison and the earlier biography is retained as history. James Glasgow-3332 remains a surviving cross-profile identity alternative for the 1624 Quothquan weaver. Its circa-1634 birth is an unsupported estimate and cannot by itself exclude that earlier man. Identification with the distinct weaver indexed at Back of Lindsaylands in 1680 would exclude a death before 1624 if established, but that later identity is itself only possible. Retain Glasgow-3910 as the record-defined 1624 account for the selected uncertain family; do not merge the profiles or transfer Glasgow-3332’s unproved parent and child attachments. The four-year difference from the 1711 baptism is between a record and an unsupported estimate, not a concrete identity conflict. This materialises the existing Scottish candidate at low confidence; it does not prove migration or two distinct elder Philips.
limitations: The Dublin records name no Scottish parents, birthplace or apprenticeship, so the Scottish child and elder watchmaker may be different men. The elder placement is a preferred working interpretation of the profile’s trade/address and family structure, not a claim that every event in that biography belongs to him. Glasco-147 is a strongly supported duplicate account of that younger man, but its quoted 1772 younger/inventory wording was not independently rechecked here and establishes neither the estimated birth nor a newly verified father clause; a grant date is not a death date. No merge, spouse transfer or new child attachment follows. Catherine Mangan is called Glasco-146’s mother in its prose but spouse in its structured family; the 1750 report describes the elder’s bride only as the widow Mangan, and the 1760 report gives no forename. Neither record proves maternity. Preserve the existing Mangan/Braccan and younger-parent fields as qualified leads; do not add a mother for Glasco-146. The 1777 probate/court occurrence does not establish survival after 1772. The local elder account uses 1772 as an uncertain death year through the selected identity, retaining the old after 1772 value and all junior events in the comparison. claim: Selected uncertain father for Older Alexander Glasgow, reconstructed Bann Valley father
basis: The same James is selected, with very low confidence, as father of the reconstructed older Alexander (Glasgow-3904). This adopts the existing possible-brother route for Adam and Alexander. On the reported 1737 and estimated 1770 years, James would be about 33 at Alexander’s birth. Making Adam, born about 1758, Alexander’s father instead produces a twelve-year interval. Alexander’s circa 1770 birth is only an estimate, so that calculation does not exclude an Adam father: Alexander could have been born later. However, fatherhood of Daniel by about 1795/96 places Alexander in a generation born by roughly 1775–1778, leaving two short successive generations in the Adam-to-Alexander model. Adam’s wife Unknown-760890, born about 1766/67 from her monument age, cannot be Alexander’s mother on that chronology. The sibling route is therefore preferred provisionally without inventing an earlier wife. Chronological economy does not prove brotherhood or a shared father; neither selected edge is independent support for the other. A 1760 lease identifies James as a Belfast ropemaker taking a ropewalk at Gardenmore, Larne; the 1768 assignment identifies the same property. This is a real occupational and locality sequence, distinct from the contemporary Larne tanner. Adam is documented much later at Inishrush, and the monument does not state his birthplace. The estimated Inishrush birth cannot exclude a family from elsewhere, but no Belfast birth or Larne-to-Inishrush migration is newly assigned. The 1773 Larne gentleman’s age excludes the younger Glasgow-3991 account; the identity assessment and separation of the two trades retain their previous grades. The reported James/Shutter-46 marriage in 1762 is later than Adam’s birth. It cannot establish Shutter-46 as Adam’s mother. An earlier union, premarital birth or inaccurate reported date would be needed if this father model is right; no such event or person is invented. Shutter-46 is not selected as older Alexander’s mother either: the marriage report and the son identity are independently unproved.
limitations: Older Alexander is himself reconstructed chiefly from late descendant testimony naming Thomas’s parents as Alexander and Rosanna. basis: John Glasgow-3375 is the selected uncertain working father of the West Kilbride parent John Glasgow-3161, through possible identity with his son Jon Glasgow-1434, indexed at Kilwinning on 6 July 1679. The West Kilbride account already names Glasgow-1434 as an identity comparison. A child born near the 1679 baptism could have been about twenty at the January 1700 Patrick event, followed by the John/Margaret Cowan children at nearby Stevenston in 1701 and 1706 if that further adult identity is right. This supplies a specific neighbouring-parish household and ordinary generation, preferred provisionally to leaving the 1700 father without a named family. It does not prove that the Kilwinning child, Stevenston father and West Kilbride father were one person.
limitations: The supplied Scotland’s People entry reads PATRICK GLASGOW, 03/01/1700, West Kilbride, parish 620, reference 10 / 27, with JOHN GLASGOW/ as the parent field. The prior source review interprets that as 3 January; the structured child field instead says 1 March. Both readings remain visible, and neither an exact birthday nor original-image inspection is claimed. The minister’s inherited circa-1680 Irish birth is unsupported by his cited career records. Taken literally, 1680 would conflict with this childhood hypothesis and with a father represented by the 1679 Kilwinning child. It remains a conflicting profile estimate, not evidence that the proposed generations fit that year. No date or birthplace is silently changed to make the route work. Scottish origin rests on a later biographical statement, not a contemporary birthplace record. Ford’s church history, printed p.16, PDF p.22, records the 1736–1741 ministry and 23 March 1753 death, but names no parent and supplies no age or birthplace. John Glasgow-551, associated with County Tyrone in the William Melanchthon Glasgow family account, remains an alternative identity already named on the West Kilbride profile. His estimated birth and the absence of a West Kilbride event do not exclude him. The Ayrshire comparison is preferred for its specific neighbouring parishes and independently indexed 1679 child, not because an Irish route has been disproved. Another local John, a brother or cousin of the Kilwinning family, or a different father remains possible. The Kilwinning-child/Stevenston-adult identity is itself uncertain. No occupation, later residence or marriage connects John-3161 to either adult. Barbara Alason/Allason is named with the 1679 child; no mother is selected for the West Kilbride account, and Margaret Cowan is not assigned as Patrick’s mother from the later Stevenston events. John-3375’s earlier family scaffold retains its existing uncertainty. Two uncertain father hypotheses are selected; both depend on unproved child/adult identities. Their combination is a conditional model, not two independent confirmations of an Ayrshire-to-Maryland descent. The corresponding child and adult accounts are retained separately without a merge; connectivity counts retained profile accounts rather than proved distinct people. No original parish image, new kinship clause, certain relationship upgrade, mother assignment or live WikiTree save is claimed. Current vital fields and confidently marked relationships are preserved, with the conflicting estimates explicitly explained.

claim: Selected uncertain father for Robert Glasgow, Carnwath and Libberton
basis: James Glasgow-3332 is the selected uncertain working father of Robert Glasgow-3407, who married Katherine Wilson at Carnwath in 1713 and is associated with son John Glasgow-2870 at Libberton in 1722. This is conditional on James representing the weaver at Back of Lindsaylands whose testament was indexed in 1680. The adjacent Biggar, Libberton and Carnwath family setting supplies a specific local comparison. A James born around the inherited 1630/1634 estimates could father Robert in the 1660s or 1670s; a Robert born in the 1670s could marry in 1713 and father John in 1722 at ordinary adult ages. This provisional older-generation route is preferred to making the two overlapping Libberton Roberts sons of the same Johne. No record names Robert as the weaver’s child. Robert’s current circa-1690 birth estimate would be too late for a father dead by 1680; an earlier birth is required if this hypothesis is right. That estimate is unsupported, but the required revision remains a limitation, not evidence for the proposed father.
limitations: The 1680 index describes James as a weaver in the Back of Lindsaylands, parish of Biggar, with indexed testament date 10 November 1680, Lanark Commissary Court CC14/5/10, TD. That is a registration date, not an exact death date. The original has not been read and supplies no reviewed Robert clause. The 1690 Edinburgh apprenticeship names a deceased father James Glasgow, weaver in Lindsayland; the matching trade and locality make him a probable instance of the indexed weaver, but identification with Glasgow-3332 remains only possible. The apprentice generation is another possible intermediary for the later family, not an additional person invented to complete a pedigree. James Glasgow-3332’s existing parentage, the separate 1648 Johne child identity, and the competing 1624 Quothquan-weaver identity retain their previous grades. The new father selection cannot itself prove any of those identities or be used circularly to reject the 1624 alternative. This particular parent model depends on the later weaver identity; the 1624 decedent would be an implausibly early direct father of this 1713–1722 household. The Carnwath marriage citation gives Robert and Katherine Wilson in 1713; the captured 1722 Libberton baptism citation names Robert and Katharin Wilson as John’s parents. Those index citations define the proposed Wilson household but supply no paternal ancestry or age for Robert. The neighbouring Robert Glasgow-4168 account combines Katherin Gibson in 1718 and Katherine Watson in 1720 and 1726. The Wilson event in 1722 falls between the Watson events. Consequently, a simple sequence of remarriages does not reconcile all maternal surnames. Transcription differences, record misassignment, overlapping families, or one man across some entries remain possible. No woman is equated with another, and no new marriage or mother is assigned. The two Robert accounts are retained separately; shared parish and forename do not prove identity. Johne Glasgow-3093 remains an unselected alternative father for the Carnwath Robert, particularly if Robert Glasgow-3407 is eventually identified with the Gibson/Watson Robert Glasgow-4168, whose selected father is already Johne. Johne’s birth around 1648 could fit fatherhood around 1690; however, no later record follows him from the Mid Calder child entry to Libberton. Giving him both Roberts would otherwise require two living sons with the same forename or an unproved identity between the accounts. The present choice avoids building that assumption into the default model. If James Glasgow-3332’s two father assignments and the Johne Glasgow-3093 to Robert Glasgow-4168 choice are right, Robert Glasgow-3407 would be the latter Robert’s paternal uncle. That is a consequence of the conditional model, not independent evidence of kinship. Another unrecorded local father and a younger Lindsaylands generation remain possible. Captain Robert Glasgow-2867 also remains a surviving identity comparison; his unsupported imported family is not a concrete exclusion, and no maritime or probate bridge identifies the Carnwath man with him. One new uncertain father is selected from existing index and family reviews. The 1680 weaver identity and an earlier Robert birth are required conditions; no new original inspection, certain relationship upgrade, mother assignment, identity merge or live WikiTree save is claimed. Existing vital fields and confidently marked metrics are unchanged. The two Robert accounts remain separate retained profiles, and no genealogical certainty is inferred from their inclusion in one working family.

basis: Patrick Glasgow-1440, represented by the Gordon Patrike baptism of 1667, is selected as a very uncertain working father of Patrick Glasgow-3920 of the Kilclone memorial. The memorial’s age 60 at death in May 1754 puts the younger Patrick’s birth around 1694. If the Gordon baptism was near birth, the older Patrick would have been about 27 then: an ordinary father–son interval. The matching Patrick/Patrike and Glasgow/Glasco name pair supplies a specific older candidate rather than an invented ancestor. This is a very weak generational model; neither name recurrence nor a feasible age establishes paternity. There is no reviewed deed, parish entry, probate clause, occupation or shared associate connecting Gordon or Stitchel to Kilclone. No migration or Scottish birthplace is newly established for the Meath man, and the catalogue is not a complete census of older Patricks.
limitations: The model keeps the two Patricks distinct. A man baptised in 1667 would have been at least about 86–87 in 1754, incompatible with the Kilclone memorial’s age 60 unless the memorial age is substantially wrong. No evidence justifies correcting that age by a generation. A father–son hypothesis fits the two dated accounts better than identifying them as one person, but another father or more distant relationship remains possible. The 1667 index names James as father of the Gordon child, not a father for the Meath Patrick. The modern James Glasgow-3107 identification and the Gordon account’s existing maternal and ancestral attachments retain their previous qualifications; this new edge does not independently prove them. The project’s reported Y-DNA affinity does not provide a named parent or establish that this particular untested Meath family belongs to a tested line. The Gordon profile also gathers Patrick’s marriage entries with Helen Fairbairn/Fairbarne at Stitchel on 23 May 1707 and Eccles on 1 July 1707, followed by children in 1708–1716. Those adult events do not themselves identify the groom with the 1667 child. If that combined identity is correct, the proposed Meath son would predate the recorded 1707 marriage by about 13 years. Helen is therefore not selected as his mother. No earlier wife, earlier marriage, illegitimacy, second household or move is invented. The proposed father would require an unrecorded earlier child, and that is a real weakness of the model. The two 1707 dates remain separate recorded entries; their precise banns/ceremony relationship has not been newly checked. The supplied Gordon index reads 4 August 1667 while the structured birth field says 8 April 1667. This existing day/month conflict remains visible, and neither index is used as proof of an exact birthday. The Kilclone inscription identifies Patrick as James’s father, and Richard and William as James’s brothers. Richard and William died on 1 November 1738; Richard’s age is 10 and William’s is printed with a query at about 7. Patrick died in May 1754 aged 60. These statements define the existing nuclear family and remain separate from the new proposed grandfather. The source used is a modern reproduction of a transcription reported in 1892, not a newly inspected photograph of the stone. The inscription supplies no mother, wife, occupation, birthplace or Scottish origin. Kilclone is the memorial context, not independent proof of Patrick’s birthplace or exact place of death. No parent-child confidence grade within the memorial family is changed. One very uncertain father is newly selected, with no mother. This is a speculative working family connection, not a proved Scotland–Meath migration or an identity merge. The age 60 memorial reading, pre 1707 child problem, uncertain adult identity of the Scottish Patrick and all prior source limitations remain explicit. No original inspection, vital-field change, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. Working connectivity counts retained profile accounts and inherits the uncertainty in older ancestry.

claim: Selected uncertain father for James Glasgow of Corvanaghan
basis: James Glasgow-1025 is selected as the very uncertain working father of James Glasgow-2988, the 1766 Corvanaghan householder, through preferred provisional identity with James Glasgow-1024 of Moneymore. The existing Corvanaghan biography already retains the Moneymore man as a compatible candidate: the places are roughly nine miles apart, the name matches and their circa 1720/1722 births are estimates rather than a real two-year conflict. The 1766 Irish occurrence can precede the compiled 1770 immigration claim associated with the Moneymore family; no post 1766 Irish occurrence has been assigned to the Corvanaghan man. This is a weak locality and chronology preference, not proof of emigration or identity. The older James is already an uncertain father in the Moneymore pedigree. Extending that attachment gives the Corvanaghan account a conditional place in the same family, without inventing an intermediate generation. It inherits two major uncertainties: adult identity and the older pedigree itself.
limitations: The older James account’s circa 1700 birth would allow an ordinary father–son interval of about 20–22 years, if the estimates are close. Those guessed years do not independently establish paternity. No contemporary record names the older James as father of either Moneymore James or the Corvanaghan householder. The current older-father attachment is a tree hypothesis, not a clause in the 1766 return, the pension record or the later family history. The older and younger James accounts might themselves be duplicates rather than father and son; if that identity is established, this additional father edge must collapse with it. Their existing Scottish ancestral attachments receive no new support. No mother is selected: the uncertain Rutherford attachment on the Moneymore account is not independently supported for the Corvanaghan man and is not copied. The 1766 Kildress return names James Glasgow as a Protestant householder at Corvanaghan. It gives no age, birthplace, wife, children, occupation or father. The two sons currently attached as James Glasgow-2989 and John Glasgow-2990 remain unproved, with their existing grades and dates unchanged. Their estimated generations cannot identify the householder. Corvanaghan is distinct from Gortnavreeghan in County Cavan; the rejected Cavan lease assignment is not restored. The 1740 Derryloran return contains two James and two William householders without townlands or kinship, and the 1766 Derryloran return separately names two Jas. Glasgo at Drumearn. None is newly assigned to a particular generation. Faris’s later genealogy calls Robert Glasgow-12’s father James of Moneymore, but the underlying evidence for that father identification has not been inspected. Robert’s 1834 pension declaration gives County Derry birth in 1749 and arrival in Virginia in 1769; it does not name parents or siblings. The fuller Mary Harkness and sibling package, the compiled 1770 entry and the 1804 same-name naturalisation applicant remain separate inherited claims. The reported departure of a mother and elder brothers by 1766 does not independently place their father in America that year. No new wife, emigrant child, ship, naturalisation identity or extreme-age death is attached to the Corvanaghan account. The 1766 return and the later Moneymore family tradition may still concern different men. James Glasgow-1970 of the Mitchell-family tradition remains a live alternative identity for the Corvanaghan householder. The 1879 Hillsdale history describes a Scotsman and his Mitchell wife moving to the Cookstown area about 1750, with a son John and later Michigan descendants. It does not name Corvanaghan. The Moneymore route is preferred only weakly for its more specific nearby locality and compatible 1766 window; the Mitchell account is not excluded, and the birthplaces on the compared profiles are not independent proof. Another local James remains possible. The absence of Glasgow occupiers at Corvanaghan in the 1826 tithe list, sixty years later, does not establish death or emigration. The 1759 will reference does not prove this father generation. The previously reviewed PRONI detail names Drumcarn, not Drumearn, and supplies no age or kin. It may concern the older account, the Moneymore James or another namesake. The meaning of 17 January 1759 and the testator’s modern profile identity remain unresolved. No 1759 death, estate event or residence is transferred to the 1766 Corvanaghan householder. The older profile’s structured dates and places are retained as existing fields with those qualifications; the new parent model does not resolve them. One very uncertain father is newly selected through a possible Moneymore identity and an already uncertain older pedigree. No mother, source-proved parentage, migration, merge, vital-field change, original inspection, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. The compared James accounts remain separate and may be duplicates rather than distinct brothers or generations. Working connectivity counts retained accounts and does not independently validate those identities. claim: Selected uncertain father for Lemuel Glasgow
basis: Caleb Glasgow-363 is selected as the very uncertain working father of Lemuel Glasgow-2581. The case combines a local surname household, a compatible older generation and the same Currituck–Pasquotank setting. Lemuel’s November 1833 pension declaration says he was born in Currituck, moved to Pasquotank as an infant and remained there until moving to Randolph about 1803. William Glasgow-428’s previously reviewed 1746 Currituck will names a son Caleb. The two modern Caleb accounts, Glasgow-363 and Glasgow-830, both cite a Pasquotank will of 1803. These details make the established local Caleb family a useful preferred home for Lemuel over an otherwise unidentified father. They do not put Caleb in Lemuel’s infant household or name his parents. The preference for Glasgow-363 is generational: its circa 1726 birth allows a father aged about 27 in 1753; Glasgow-830’s circa 1740 birth would give about 13. Neither Caleb birth is established by a birth record here, and Lemuel himself said he had no age record and only believed he was born in 1753. The younger estimate therefore lowers the second account’s preference without excluding it. No baptism, guardianship, deed or pension statement names Caleb as Lemuel’s father. A collateral connection to Caleb, another local Glasgow father or an unrelated Glasgow immigrant remains possible. This is a low-confidence named-family hypothesis, not a documented father clause.
limitations: The Caleb profiles may represent one man with conflicting dates rather than brothers. Both point to the same FamilySearch person K815-XBS and the same family-site account; those references are not independent corroboration. Glasgow-363 records 1781 as his death year but its biography transcribes a Pasquotank will dated 20 September 1803; Glasgow-830 places Caleb’s death in 1804 and probate in 1808. The 1803 transcription names children Barhnda (as transcribed), James, Dorcas and Nancy, and an unnamed wife, but not Lemuel. That omission weakens a father hypothesis if this is the relevant testator, without proving that an older, separately established son could not have been omitted. No reason for an omission is established. The will’s modern-profile identity remains unresolved and neither death estimate is changed. Glasgow-830 remains an explicit unselected alternative father account, especially if its approximate birth is wrong or it is a duplicate of Glasgow-363. No merge or second selected father is made. The 1746 son Caleb cannot yet be assigned uniquely between the two profiles from the will’s name alone. The existing Caleb children and the apparent duplicate Jesse accounts retain their current links and grades; this batch does not resolve their identities. The newly selected edge joins Lemuel’s two-child family to the existing working tree while retaining the uncertainty of the older Currituck pedigree. William Glasgow-428 is not selected as Lemuel’s father: the previously reviewed probate was in April 1747, roughly six years before Lemuel’s believed 1753 birth. The 1746 will’s expected unborn child cannot normally be a child born in 1753. Making William the father would require a material error in Lemuel’s recollected birth, for which this review supplies no evidence. William’s own father Daniel remains unproved by the inspected records; no certainty is added to that older connection. No mother is selected for Lemuel. Gregory-3163’s existing attachment to Caleb and the Ruth Sawyer name in the other Caleb biography do not identify Lemuel’s mother. Dauge-19’s recorded 1715 birth also conflicts with literal maternity of a child born in 1726; that inherited chronology needs its own review rather than being silently repaired here. One very uncertain father is newly selected. No mother, merge, new person, changed vital field, original manuscript inspection, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. The Caleb accounts remain separate pending identity review. Working connectivity measures retained profile accounts and selected hypotheses; they do not prove either the paternity or a unique historical person count. The confidently marked connectivity totals remain unchanged.

evidence_grade: Probable father inferred from the combined Duddingston family and Edinburgh craft records
claim: Robert of Duddingston is probably the Edinburgh weaver James’s father
basis: Robert Glasgow-1156 is now assessed as the probable father of James Glasgow-1150, the Edinburgh weaver. Grant’s 16 June 1641 apprenticeship names James’s father Robert and places the entry at Wester Duddingston with William Crichtoun and master William Sclaitter. The 20 June 1649 burgess admission repeats Sclaitter’s name and the exact apprenticeship date, securely connecting the recorded son to the adult weaver. The Robert buried at Duddingston on 17 January 1647 fits the father’s name, parish and preceding generation, six years after the apprenticeship and before James’s independent household began in 1649. Taken together, the specific local father and the Duddingston burial favour one Robert over an otherwise unattested second contemporary Robert in that parish. The previous assessment treated the lack of a unique identifier as a reason to stop at plausible; the combined argument warrants probable, while remaining an inference.
limitations: The apprenticeship proves James’s father was Robert; identifying that father with the burial account Glasgow-1156 is probable rather than documented. The burial index gives no age, son, wife or occupation, and burial in the parish does not itself prove residence at Wester Duddingston. A second local Robert remains possible. The two craft entries are a linked identity chain, not two independent statements naming the father. The exact scope of “servitor” in the printed apprenticeship wording need not decide the inference: the entry supplies the father’s name and Duddingston association. No mother is identified, so Deborah Ivey is not upgraded. Robert’s unsupported Archibald-1097 ancestry and his compatible identification with Andrew-3163’s recorded son Robert-4006 remain separate questions. Neither the later Fisherrow sasine identity nor the Edinburgh weaver’s possible Lindsaylands continuation is needed for this father conclusion.

evidence_grade: Probable parentage from explicit descendant testimony and independently matching emigrant household
claim: Hugh Glasgow, elder Irish weaver is probably the father of Hugh Glasgow, Pennsylvania emigrant
basis: Hugh Glasgow-548 and Margaret McCullough-1964 are assessed as the probable parents of Hugh Glasgow-540, the emigrant whose Pennsylvania will was made in 1827 and proved in 1831. William Melanchthon Glasgow’s family history, p.2, explicitly names the elder Hugh and Margaret as the married parents of John, Robert and their youngest son Hugh, born in County Londonderry in 1739. Page 3 follows this younger Hugh’s household through John, whom the author calls his grandfather, and its emigration in 1796. This is specific descendant testimony about a named family, rather than a parent invented from dates or a shared surname. The younger Hugh’s recorded will independently names the same four sons John, Hugh, Alexander and Robert, and daughter Nancy, within the corresponding Pennsylvania household. That agreement supports the family history’s identification of the emigrant and the reliability of its nearer family relationships. It does not independently name his parents. The explicit family account, consistent household identity and feasible generations together warrant probable parentage rather than leaving the father and mother ungraded.
limitations: Parentage rests on one retrospective family account; later online copies and family trees are derivatives, not independent witnesses. Its author gives no Irish baptism or marriage source, and its 1824 death claim is contradicted by Hugh’s signed 1827 will and 1831 probate. The 1733 marriage, 1739 birth, older Hugh’s circa-1706 birth and Margaret’s imported vital estimates retain their separate evidence limits. The two adult Hugh Glasgow householders in Tamlaght O’Crilly in 1740 support an earlier local surname generation, but the return supplies no kin or townland. Entry 1272 remains a leading compatible identity for the elder Hugh; collector order beside Ellis and McCullough names is not proof of adjoining homes or of Margaret’s father. No particular 1740 householder or the 1772 subscriber is selected as this man. The 1827 will does not name the testator’s parents or his wife; it therefore cannot independently establish Margaret’s maternity or Sally Blair’s identity. No John-551 parentage, older William/Covenanter ancestry, Cameron origin story, or connection to Adam of Inishrush is upgraded. The two brothers retain their existing links and grades: John-549’s captured confident flags are not counted as new upgrades, and Robert-550’s separate life remains unverified.

evidence_grade: Probable parentage from explicit descendant testimony and independently matching emigrant household
claim: Margaret McCullough is probably the mother of Hugh Glasgow, Pennsylvania emigrant
basis: Hugh Glasgow-548 and Margaret McCullough-1964 are assessed as the probable parents of Hugh Glasgow-540, the emigrant whose Pennsylvania will was made in 1827 and proved in 1831. William Melanchthon Glasgow’s family history, p.2, explicitly names the elder Hugh and Margaret as the married parents of John, Robert and their youngest son Hugh, born in County Londonderry in 1739. Page 3 follows this younger Hugh’s household through John, whom the author calls his grandfather, and its emigration in 1796. This is specific descendant testimony about a named family, rather than a parent invented from dates or a shared surname. The younger Hugh’s recorded will independently names the same four sons John, Hugh, Alexander and Robert, and daughter Nancy, within the corresponding Pennsylvania household. That agreement supports the family history’s identification of the emigrant and the reliability of its nearer family relationships. It does not independently name his parents. The explicit family account, consistent household identity and feasible generations together warrant probable parentage rather than leaving the father and mother ungraded.
limitations: Parentage rests on one retrospective family account; later online copies and family trees are derivatives, not independent witnesses. Its author gives no Irish baptism or marriage source, and its 1824 death claim is contradicted by Hugh’s signed 1827 will and 1831 probate. The 1733 marriage, 1739 birth, older Hugh’s circa-1706 birth and Margaret’s imported vital estimates retain their separate evidence limits. The two adult Hugh Glasgow householders in Tamlaght O’Crilly in 1740 support an earlier local surname generation, but the return supplies no kin or townland. Entry 1272 remains a leading compatible identity for the elder Hugh; collector order beside Ellis and McCullough names is not proof of adjoining homes or of Margaret’s father. No particular 1740 householder or the 1772 subscriber is selected as this man. The 1827 will does not name the testator’s parents or his wife; it therefore cannot independently establish Margaret’s maternity or Sally Blair’s identity. No John-551 parentage, older William/Covenanter ancestry, Cameron origin story, or connection to Adam of Inishrush is upgraded. The two brothers retain their existing links and grades: John-549’s captured confident flags are not counted as new upgrades, and Robert-550’s separate life remains unverified.

evidence_grade: Probable father: explicit family-history attribution extended across established brothers
claim: James Glasgow, Moneymore father account is probably the father of Robert Glasgow, Adams County emigrant
basis: The existing Moneymore father account, Glasgow-1024, is assessed as the probable father of Robert Glasgow-12 and, by inference through their established brotherhood, Arthur Glasgow-649 and Joseph Glasgow-1543. The catalogue description of David Faris’s 1990 genealogy explicitly identifies the Adams County emigrant Robert (1749–1839) as a son of a James resident at Moneymore. It identifies a particular father and son, rather than offering a same-name local candidate. The family letter of 6 November 1806 printed by Faris names Arthur and Robert as Joseph’s brothers; Joseph’s 1831 will independently identifies Arthur as his deceased brother and the younger Robert as Arthur’s son. These sources distinguish the two Roberts and establish the sibling group to which the father attribution can reasonably extend. Robert’s pension supports the County Derry setting and 1769 migration. The approximate generations are compatible; the circa-1722 birth estimate is not independent evidence. The positive father attribution and established family group together warrant probable parentage, while remaining below documented or certain.
limitations: The father attribution survives here through a catalogue abstract of a retrospective genealogy; the book’s underlying parentage notes and a contemporary Irish parent record have not been inspected. The letter and will corroborate the sibling group, not the father’s name independently. Glasgow-1024 is used for its record-defined Moneymore father role: the inherited dates, Mary Harkness marriage, 1770 immigration, 1804 naturalisation, older James pedigree and proposed Corvanaghan identity are separate questions. The Corvanaghan identity and older father remain very uncertain. No probability is assigned to those claims by this review. The same father is inferred across the three established paternal-surname siblings; no evidence for different fathers has been identified. Other proposed siblings, including James-3305, John and Mary, and the proposed Adam connection are not upgraded.

evidence_grade: Probable father; Murieston family reconstruction
basis: Prefer the named George of Mureistoun as James Glasgow-991’s probable father. George is recorded at Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder obligation; the accepted 1605 original-register reading places James’s household in probable Muirestoun and names an adult George Glasgow as witness to the baptism of James’s son George. The earlier review already assessed the two adult George occurrences as probably one man. The same uncommon surname, the probable same holding across nineteen years, and the older name-bearer’s personal participation in the younger household favour lineal family continuity. Father is the preferred degree: an older established man followed by James’s child-bearing household is a normal two-generation sequence, and the child’s George name is compatible with that reconstruction. This is a combined locality/household inference, not three independent proofs or a compulsory naming rule.
limitations: The 1605 witness’s residence and age are unstated, and Muirestoun remains a probable reading/location. Shared holding names do not prove a legal title transfer. Father, uncle, older brother, cousin and neighbour remain genuine alternatives. The 1586 obligation does not establish muster attendance, and neither record states that George was James’s father. The George name and witness role are supporting context, not direct kinship. Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains an unselected uncertain father alternative; his 1597/8 testament names Robert, Marion, Jonet and Isobel, not James. The George comparison supplies a closer holding-and-witness association than the broader Andrew/Calder model, without proving that Andrew could not be James’s father.

profile_names.Glasgow-1970: James Glasgow of the Cookstown Mitchell family

evidence_grade: Uncertain working father; existing identity comparison
basis: Select James Glasgow-1970 of the Cookstown Mitchell family as John Glasgow-2539 of Gortin’s uncertain working father, through the existing possible identification with John Glasgow-1968. The 1879 Hillsdale history specifically identifies James and his Mitchell wife as parents of John, a farmer near Cookstown. The Gortin account supplies another John in the same Derryloran/Cookstown locality and an earlier compatible father generation. The maintained Hillsdale research already lists Gortin John as a possible duplicate. This is a positive named-son comparison in the relevant family and locality, stronger than an arbitrary father chosen only from the surname. Prefer this existing family as a revisable home for the 17-profile Gortin branch; retain both John accounts separately.
limitations: The identity is uncertain. The Hillsdale histories describe John and Jane’s seven children as Robert, Mary A., William, John, Bessie, James and Margaret; the Gortin account instead links Francis, Hugh, Letitia and Samuel. No child has been matched across those sets. An earlier union could explain different couple-based lists, but none is established here and no additional marriage is invented. If the seven-child account was intended as an exhaustive lifetime list for John, the extra Gortin group would conflict with it. The Gortin before-1771 birth boundary comes from Samuel’s reported 1792 birth; the Hillsdale c.1778 father estimate is younger. Literal 1778 fatherhood of a 1792 child would be about 14 and is a serious constraint. These are reconstructed ages and estimates, not two original birth entries; both are retained, without silently shifting either date. Sarah MacNeece’s status as the Gortin man’s widow and Jane’s identity also require testing; no mother is transferred to Gortin John and no wife is added or replaced. Another local John, a collateral relationship, or different father remain alternatives. The 1700s and 1800s family accounts do not independently prove these two Johns identical.

The father’s repeated full name, the neighbouring Berwickshire parishes, the first child three years after marriage and the orderly thirteen-year child sequence form a coherent family. The daughter Agnes supplies modest naming support; it is not the deciding evidence. The maintained 1702 Gordon marriage citation for Jean also names father James, adding a compatible adult continuation for her. Read together, these favour a single local family over six isolated fathers or an unrelated Polwarth couple. No concrete competing contemporary Gordon James household has been identified in the maintained material. That is the scope of this comparison, not a claim to have exhausted the population.
limitations: The child indexes explicitly name James as father but omit the mother. Their named-father roles are documented for the record-defined children; identifying that father with the 1663 Polwarth husband is probable. Agnes Watt is separately assessed as probable mother of all six children on the marriage, locality and sustained family sequence. This is an inference, not literal maternity in the indexes; a later marriage or another local James remains possible. Jean’s later marriage and the later adult identities of John and Patrick remain separately assessed. Patrick’s proposed Kilclone son and migration, James’s own John Glasgow-1084 ancestry and the unrelated Kilwaughter James are not strengthened. No original register image was newly inspected: this review combines the previously accepted index entries and maintained citations. The unchanged paternal working branch below James contains 43 pre-1850 retained profile accounts. This count includes uncertain later identities and the speculative Gordon–Kilclone join; it is not 43 proved descendants. The 1666 John account lacked Agnes as a mother; the local tree now adds her as probable, extending the same assessed household across all six children. The other five maternal attachments are retained and explicitly graded. One saved maternal flag was already confident, but the reviewed source does not name a mother: the local assessment is probable and the saved flag remains separately visible. Three father flags were already confident and are confirmations, not new certainty upgrades. Date/place conflicts are preserved for source checking: John’s structured Duns location versus the cited Gordon baptism; Patrick’s 8 April field versus the 4 August index; Robert’s 4 January field versus the 1 April index. No birth date, place, father attachment, spouse, merge or live WikiTree flag changes. The named-parent conclusion must not silently certify those conflicting vital fields or any later migration.

claim: Selected uncertain Quothquan working father for Whitecastle James
basis: Select John Glasgow-1086 of Quothquan as the uncertain local working father of James Glasgow-1376. The choice is conditional on the Whitecastle man’s possible identity with James Glasgow-3332, provisionally compared with the weaver at Back of Lindsaylands whose testament was indexed in 1680. The newly supported probable Clydesdale setting supplies a positive regional bridge that the earlier review lacked. The same name, neighbouring Libberton/Biggar households and compatible adult dates favour that existing local account as the leading identity comparison. The 1690 apprentice entry names a deceased James Glasgow, weaver in Lindsayland, as father of the apprentice; that trade and place probably identify the 1680 testator, not the Whitecastle man directly. John is already the uncertain father attached to James-3332. Carry that family placement across the possible identity at its actual uncertainty, rather than inventing another father. John’s possible 1608 childhood would fit a son born in the 1630s–1650s; neither James birth estimate is a recorded age. This is a selected, revisable family hypothesis, not a parent clause in the 1672 decree.
limitations: There are two dependent gaps: Whitecastle James is not proved to be the Lindsaylands weaver, and John’s paternity of James-3332 is itself unproved. John’s 1685 Quothquan testament names his widow but no child; the absence of James, if dead by 1680, would not exclude this model. James-3332’s possible identity with the 1624 weaver would invalidate this particular later-life route, because the 1624 decedent cannot be the man present in 1672. James-1150, the Edinburgh weaver, remains an alternative adult identification for the later weaver rather than being excluded from an unsupported birth estimate; another local James or a different kinship degree remains possible. The old Marion-baptism role error supplies no positive parentage for James-1376, and the Duffe household James-2682 is not merged. The 1738 Edinburgh Castle lead is unselected and incompatible with a death by 1680 if this weaver identity is right. No 1680 original was newly read: the maintained case has only the supplied wills index, and no linked manuscript or transcription. Neither a marriage nor a mother is supplied. Jonet Kinnie, John’s widow, is not automatically James’s mother. Keep both James profiles separate; they may represent one man, not two proved brothers.
model_note: The printed decree in Robert Wodrow’s 1721 History, volume I, appendix no. XLVII, pp.133–134, is dated 27 July 1672 in both its heading and Latin opening. It names “James Glasgow in Whitecastle” among people imprisoned for refusing the oath. The monetary fines there belong to Mr James Duncan and the Countess of Wigtoun, not to James Glasgow. William Crookshank’s 1751 summary, volume I p.285, places the same named group under 24 July 1672; preserve that day discrepancy and prefer the printed decree’s 27 July for this source account. Neither source supports the old 1670 date. The two books recount the same proceeding and are not independent evidence of two imprisonments. The surrounding Biggar/Boghall group names men in Biggar, Carwood, Edmonstoun, Worslyd and Carstairs. This favours the Whitecastle in Libberton parish over a location guessed merely from general Covenanter activity. J. L. Davidson’s published article title locates West Whitecastle Farm in Libberton, Lanarkshire (Proceedings of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland 108, p.383; title checked in the journal’s search-indexed contents, full article not inspected). claim: John Glasgow of Kirkliston may be a child of Thomas Glasgow.
basis: Select Thomas Glasgow-1023 and Janet Mill-357 as possible working parents of John Glasgow-159, each at 42%, conditional on the Kirkliston husband being the John represented by Glasgow-2980 at Mid Calder in 1750. The Mid Calder account already identifies that named couple. A man recorded in 1750 could marry in 1785 at about 35 and father the Kirkliston children in 1786–1797. The catalogue’s circa-1761 birth for the husband is an unsupported estimate, not an age that excludes him. Mid Calder/Livingston and Kirkliston form a compatible Lothian labouring-family route. The first recorded son Thomas (1786) and later daughter Janet (1790) repeat both proposed parents’ names, giving this couple a modest positive advantage over the other local John households.
limitations: The identifying step is an inference: no inspected record takes the 1750 child to Kirkliston or names the husband’s parents. The Thomas/Janet naming fit is supporting context, not a compulsory naming rule or two independent proofs. John-3581 (Kirknewton 1755, John/Mary Robertson), John-3480 (Kirknewton/East Calder 1751, John/Christian Meek) and John-2846 (West Calder 1747, John/Margaret Anderson) all remain compatible. Their blank later lives do not exclude them. John-1304’s estimated 1771 childhood and Muckle household make him a weaker comparison, without proving that the estimate or any first-marriage assumption is right. Another unindexed John remains possible. The 1750 FamilySearch index citations were reused from maintained captures; this review reached the provider’s sign-in page and did not inspect the original register. The two index URLs refer to one event, not independent corroboration. John-2980 and John-159 remain separate accounts that may represent one man; the selected parents do not establish two distinct sons named John. The husband’s birth field stays circa 1761, explicitly unproved, until identity is resolved. Thomas’s Kilwinning childhood and the family’s earlier ancestry are separate inherited identifications and are not strengthened. The same 42% applies to each parent because both depend on that one child-to-adult identity; these are not independent probabilities.

claim: Possible Stichill father for Robert of Leitholm, 34%
basis: Select James Glasgow (Glasgow-1238), the father recorded with Elizabath/Elizabeth Tait at Stichill, as Robert Glasgow’s possible working father, at 34%. The couple’s maintained marriage citation is dated 25 January 1740; their David and James children are indexed in June 1744 and July 1746. Robert’s estimated 1745 birth fits that family generation and could fall between those events; it is not a dated baptism. Stichill and Eccles/Leitholm belong to the same small Borders district, and the later Swinton entry attributed to the James/Tait couple offers a further local comparison. Robert’s earlier son James supplies a modest naming clue consistent with this father; a common forename cannot establish paternity. The combination favours this existing, record-defined family over the catalogue’s distant Kirknewton candidates, whose apparent proximity came from mapping Leitholm to South Leith. No inspected record names Robert as James’s son.
limitations: This is a preferred, revisable hypothesis, with 34% subjective confidence, not a measured probability or a confident connection. Robert’s 1745 birth and 8 August 1800 death each have zero attached sources on the inspected FamilySearch tree. Neither date establishes an age or place of birth. The local 1745 estimate is retained unchanged. FamilySearch attaches John Glasgow (1720–1785, GFNP-FS8) and Agnes Spark (1722–deceased, K8CD-HCW) as parents; retain that alternative without treating a contributed tree as documentary proof. The evidential basis of that parent attachment has not yet been reviewed. Do not equate that John with the much older John Glasgow-1057, husband of Agnes Spark-330, from the matching names alone. James’s brother John Glasgow-1444, christened at Stichill in 1708, is another compatible local father-generation alternative with no presently inspected Robert link. An unrecorded local father or another kinship degree remains possible. The Swinton/1740 couple continuity and Robert’s own early life need testing. Elizabeth Tait is not selected as Robert’s mother: her marriage and maternity of other children do not identify his mother. Robert is not merged with an earlier child, and James’s existing older ancestry retains its own uncertainty.

claim: Possible Dalziel father of the Cambusnethan John, 41%
basis: Select James Glasgow of the 1719 Dalziel record (Glasgow-3523) as John Glasgow-3094’s possible working father, at 41% subjective confidence. This joins the Cambusnethan John-and-Ann family provisionally to the adjacent Dalziel James-and-Samuel family. The positive comparison combines a particular nearby surname household, a viable parent generation, and John’s two currently listed sons James and Samuel repeating the older two given names. Samuel is a more discriminating comparison than John or James alone. The proposed sequence is Samuel to James to John to the later James and Samuel; only the first and last household roles have cited baptismal support. No record names the adult John’s father or shows the 1719 child’s later life. The 41% rates that whole immediate-father proposition, including the child-to-adult identity gap; it is comparative judgment, not a measured frequency or a probability for the complete pedigree.
limitations: John’s 1770 birth is an uncertain profile estimate, not a baptism or recorded age. If taken literally with 1719 it implies fatherhood at about 51, which is possible and supplies no maternity information. An illustrative John birth in 1750–1770 would give a James age of about 31–51 and a 1790 groom aged 20–40; neither range is adopted as a new date. The 15 March 1719 index date is not independently established as a birthday. The named James may have died young or belonged to another later household. Adjacency does not prove continuity, and an interval of roughly seventy years separates the two parish events. James and Samuel are the currently attached children, not a proved complete or birth-ordered family. Samuel could come from Ann Clerk’s family or another relative; no Scottish naming rule determines the father. The family names and the existing father assignment to Samuel are not independent demonstrations of John’s ancestry. Retain another local James or another unrepresented father, and a collateral relationship to the Dalziel family. Samuel Glasgow-3166 is an alternative direct father if John was substantially older than the 1770 estimate; the ordinary younger-groom generation favours an intervening James, but the absent age cannot exclude an older groom. The earlier Calder Alexander/Clerk-marriage comparison remains a possible wider ancestry route, not a proved direct father: repeated Clerk marriages do not identify Ann’s family or establish a two-century pedigree. Other Scottish James households are not excluded for missing fields, but no comparably specific Cambusnethan–Dalziel and James/Samuel sequence was found in the bounded local catalogue comparison. James’s mother and wife remain unknown. No mother is selected for John, and no relationship is inferred between Ann Clerk and the earlier Clerk women. Preserve the existing ungraded Samuel-to-James father mark and all current child-parent grades, without a confidence upgrade or live save. The 1690s–1794 London pen-cutter comparison for Samuel remains very weak and separate; it supplies no evidence for this family. No person is merged, created or redated.

claim: Selected probable father for the1696 apprentice,76%
basis: Select the Edinburgh weaver and burgess James Glasgow-1150 as the probable father of the record-defined 1696 apprentice James Glasgow-4114, at 76% subjective confidence. Printed page 37 names the apprentice’s father as James Glasgow, weaver and burgess. Name, occupation, civic status and Edinburgh setting identify a particular established craftsman rather than just a same-name Scottish father. The maintained 1641 apprenticeship and 1649 burgess cross-reference securely establish James-1150 as a weaver and burgess; printed page 72 also records a James Glasgow, weaver and burgess, taking John Paterson as apprentice on 18 October 1693. The maintained burgess-roll review found one matching admission, although an index cannot rule out another man. This makes James-1150 the preferred father-profile match. The child account itself is defined by the 22 April 1696 entry, so no later-life identification is needed for that child.
limitations: The 76% is an individual research judgment for the whole father-profile identification, not a measured frequency. The published entry proves a father called James, weaver and burgess; it does not supply his apprenticeship date, wife, home address or age. Another matching craftsman, including a Lindsaylands man who also held burgess rights, remains possible. The circa-1680 child date and circa-1620 father date are estimates, not recorded ages; the nominal sixty-year interval makes late fatherhood relevant but is not a contradiction. James’s 1641 apprenticeship supplies no exact birth year. The younger James’s mother remains unknown: neither Bessie Whyte nor Agnes Duncan is transferred merely because she married the proposed father. The father’s existing probable Robert ancestry and all other family grades remain unchanged. The earlier claim that the 1690 and 1696 apprentices must be different men is withdrawn. The 1690 entry explicitly calls its Lindsayland weaver father deceased and says that the apprenticeship was scored out. The 1696 entry omits a death qualification; silence does not prove that father alive. A cancelled cordiner apprenticeship followed by an apothecary apprenticeship six years later is compatible with one man, although not established. The matching apprentice/father names and father’s weaving trade support testing that possibility; burgess status is given only for the 1696 father and the two masters differ. Keep the two existing profiles distinct pending an identifier; do not create them again. This alternative limits the father assessment rather than being erased.

The archived chronology explicitly places a James, son of Hugh, at New Town/Larne in 1737 and identifies its reported 1762 Janet Shutter groom with that James. Hugh is an independently documented Larne merchant and elder, jointly leasing Newtown property in1736 and dealing with Hugh Shutter in the original1749 mortgage. The later James/Janet account and the distinctive Jane Shutter name in the younger William’s monument fit a recurring Glasgow–Shutter network. These combined named-parent, locality, generation and family-association clues favour Hugh over retaining a William father without a named-son record.

The chronology is one derivative reconstruction: its1737 child,1762 groom and reported1737–1802 stone must not be counted as three independent confirmations. The adult’s1737 birth may itself derive from that reconstruction; the independent1773 affidavit establishes only birth before27 October1743. The original1737 entry,1762 marriage and alleged James/Janet stone remain uninspected. Hugh Shutter’s relationship to Janet is unknown, and a business association does not identify a father-in-law. Do not equate the two James profiles, invent a second wife, or infer surviving brothers with the same forename as an established fact. The older ropemaker was already an adult in1760–1761 and over thirty in1773, so he remains distinct from the younger monument/tanner comparison. One selected father is replaced locally. No birth, death, parents or childhood identity is assigned to Lillias from the contributed 1766 estimate.

basis: John Glasgow-1022 is an unselected father candidate for the Glenleslie Robert represented within Glasgow-1367, assessed at 18% subjective confidence. The 1851 transcription places Antrim-born Glasgow farmers John, reported 99, and Robert, 72, in Glenleslie houses 21 and 23, with the Hamill household between them. Their approximately 27-year age gap fits fatherhood better than an ordinary sibling interval. However, the transcription defines field 17 as the year of first marriage and gives John 1791. Robert’s census-implied birth about 1778–1779 precedes that by roughly twelve years. Earlier fatherhood would therefore require nonmarital fatherhood, incomplete reporting or a wrong age/date; none is established. Locality, surname, farming and generation also fit collateral kin. John remains the leading named local father comparison, while an unidentified father is more likely overall.
